prompt: A team says its multiplatform tool "converts" one app into a native Android app and a native iOS app. What does the lesson say about that picture?

choices.text: It is how Kotlin Multiplatform works, for screens
choices.why: Kotlin Multiplatform shares logic, and the screens stay native unless Compose Multiplatform is added.

choices.text: It is how React Native works
choices.why: React Native runs JavaScript in the app and asks the platform for views at runtime; nothing is converted into Kotlin or Swift.

choices.text: No tool converts; each approach decides which parts run on both phones
choices.why: Right. The four approaches differ in what is written once, and none of them translates an app into two.

choices.text: It is true of Capacitor, which compiles the HTML
choices.why: Capacitor shows the page in a WebView; the HTML stays HTML.

prompt: Match each approach to what is written once in it.
right_distractors: the screens, but not the logic

prompt: What makes a progressive web app different from a Capacitor app?

choices.text: There is no app package: the browser installs a website
choices.why: Right. A Capacitor app is a native package with a WebView inside; a PWA is the website itself, on the home screen.

choices.text: It draws with the platform's own views
choices.why: A PWA runs in the browser, so the browser draws it.

choices.text: It is written in Dart
choices.why: That is Flutter. A PWA is HTML, CSS and JavaScript, like a wrapped site.

choices.text: It reaches more device features than a wrapper, because it needs no plugins
choices.why: The other way round: it reaches only what the browser allows, and a wrapper's plugins reach further.

prompt: A bug in the rule that decides which week a session falls in is fixed in the Android app. In which approach is it still waiting in the iOS app?

choices.text: Kotlin Multiplatform
choices.why: There the rule is written once in shared Kotlin, so the fix reaches both.

choices.text: React Native
choices.why: One JavaScript codebase serves both phones, so the fix is in both.

choices.text: A Capacitor wrapper
choices.why: Both apps show the same website, rule included.

choices.text: Native, Kotlin and Swift
choices.why: Right. Every rule is written twice, so a fix in one is not in the other.

prompt: Which of the four approaches are the three options of the track's fork after this course?

choices.text: Flutter, Kotlin Multiplatform and Capacitor
choices.why: None of those is a route in this track; react-native and front-multiplatform look at them.

choices.text: Native for Android, native for iOS, and React Native
choices.why: Right: Android with Kotlin, iOS with Swift, and multiplatform with React Native.

choices.text: React Native, Flutter and a PWA
choices.why: Only React Native is a route; the other two routes are native.

choices.text: Native, Kotlin Multiplatform and web wrappers
choices.why: Kotlin Multiplatform and wrappers are not routes of this track.

prompt: In a React Native app, what is a <Button> on the screen of an Android phone?

choices.text: Pixels React Native painted with its own engine
choices.why: That is Flutter's model, not React Native's.

choices.text: An Android button, created at runtime
choices.why: Right. React Native's documentation says it creates the corresponding Android and iOS views.

choices.text: An HTML button inside a WebView
choices.why: That would be a wrapper. React Native has no page and no DOM.

choices.text: A Material button that Flutter lends to React Native through a platform channel
choices.why: The two toolkits do not lend each other anything; a platform channel is Flutter's way to platform code.

prompt: Apple changes the look of iOS buttons in a new release, and no app is updated. Which app shows the new look?

choices.text: The Flutter app, because Impeller follows the system
choices.why: Impeller is shipped inside the app, and Flutter draws its own widgets; they change when Flutter and the app are updated.

choices.text: Both the Flutter app and the React Native app
choices.why: Only one of them uses the system's own buttons.

choices.text: Neither, until both are rebuilt against the new SDK
choices.why: A platform view is drawn by the system that is on the phone now.

choices.text: The React Native app
choices.why: Right. Its buttons are the platform's views, so they change with the system.

prompt: Why does the lesson say that Kotlin Multiplatform "does not draw at all"?

choices.text: It shares code below the screen, and the team chooses what draws on top
choices.why: Right: native views on each side, or Compose Multiplatform on both.

choices.text: Because its apps have no interface
choices.why: Its apps have screens; Kotlin Multiplatform is just not what draws them.

choices.text: Because it hands drawing to a WebView
choices.why: That is a wrapper.

choices.text: Because Kotlin cannot run on iOS
choices.why: It compiles the same Kotlin for iOS; that is the point of it.

prompt: Match each approach to where its code runs on the phone.

pairs.right: a JavaScript engine shipped in the app

right_distractors: a server the app calls for every screen

prompt: A designer wants the planner to look identical, pixel for pixel, on an Android phone and an iPhone. Which approach gives that with the least work?

choices.text: React Native, since one codebase draws both
choices.why: One codebase, but the views are each platform's, so a button looks Android on Android and iOS on iOS.

choices.text: Native, with the same design given to both teams
choices.why: Two toolkits drawing the same design is two implementations to keep matching, which is the most work.

choices.text: Flutter
choices.why: Right. It paints every pixel itself, so both phones show the same drawing unless the app asks otherwise.

choices.text: Kotlin Multiplatform with native screens
choices.why: Native screens are the two platforms' own, so they differ.

prompt: Match each approach to its way across to platform code.
A Kotlin Multiplatform project declares a function with expect in the common code and gives an actual only for Android. What happens?

choices.text: The build fails for iOS
choices.why: Right. The compiler checks that every expected declaration has an actual in every platform.

choices.text: The iOS app crashes when the function is called
choices.why: It never gets that far: the missing half is a build error.

choices.text: The iOS app uses the Android implementation
choices.why: Android code does not run on iOS.

choices.text: The function returns null on iOS, silently
choices.why: There is no silent default; the compiler refuses.

prompt: In a Flutter platform channel, a Dart Map is sent to the iOS side. What does Swift receive?

choices.text: The same Dart object, shared in memory
choices.why: The data is serialised by the channel's codec and rebuilt on the other side.

choices.text: A JSON string Swift has to parse by hand
choices.why: The codec does the conversion; Swift receives its own type.

choices.text: A Dictionary
choices.why: Right. The codec turns a Map into a HashMap in Kotlin or a Dictionary in Swift.

choices.text: A HashMap
choices.why: That is what Kotlin receives on Android.

prompt: A React Native team needs a sensor Apple added this year, and no library supports it yet. What does the team have to write?

choices.text: Nothing; React Native reaches every iOS API from JavaScript
choices.why: JavaScript cannot call an iOS API directly; something has to cross the border.

choices.text: A native module, with its iOS half in Swift
choices.why: Right. The far side of the border is written in the platform's language, here by the team itself.

choices.text: A web page that asks the browser for the sensor
choices.why: There is no page in a React Native app.

choices.text: A platform channel in Dart
choices.why: That is Flutter's mechanism, in Flutter's language.

prompt: Put the steps of adding a Turbo Native Module to a React Native app in order.
items: write a typed specification in TypeScript or Flow
let Codegen turn it into native interfaces
call it from the app's JavaScript
write the Kotlin and Swift halves against the interfaces

prompt: Why does a native Kotlin app have no border to cross to reach the camera?

choices.text: Android gives native apps a faster camera
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; there is simply nothing in between.

choices.text: Compose includes a camera component
choices.why: The point is the language, not a component.

choices.text: The camera needs no permission in a native app
choices.why: Every approach asks for the camera; the permission is the platform's.

choices.text: Its code is already in the platform's language
choices.why: Right. There is no shared code, so Kotlin calls the Android API directly.

prompt: What does the lesson say about the Kotlin, Swift and React Native fragments of the week's line?

choices.text: They were run on an emulator and a simulator
choices.why: There is no emulator, simulator or phone on the recording machine.

choices.text: They are the output of one tool, in three languages
choices.why: Each was written in its own toolkit's style; no tool produced them.

choices.text: They were not compiled or run, and are there to be recognised
choices.why: Right. They are adapted from each toolkit's documentation, to read one idea in three spellings.

choices.text: Only the React Native one was run, because it is TypeScript
choices.why: React Native needs its own runtime and a phone or simulator; none was run.

prompt: Which are true of all three fragments? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The screen is described as a function of the total
choices.why: Yes: each takes a total and describes the screen for it.

choices.text: A text is stacked above a button
choices.why: Yes: Column, VStack and View.

choices.text: Each imports weekTotal from planner.ts
choices.why: Only the React Native one runs JavaScript and can import it.

choices.text: The button is the same Material button on both phones
choices.why: The SwiftUI one is an iOS button, and React Native's becomes each phone's own.

prompt: A team writes the planner natively in Compose and SwiftUI, and wants weekTotal written only once. What does the lesson point to?

choices.text: Kotlin Multiplatform, so both screens get it from shared Kotlin
choices.why: Right. The screens stay native and the sum is written once.

choices.text: Importing planner.ts into the Swift app
choices.why: Swift does not run TypeScript.

choices.text: A WebView that runs planner.ts on each screen
choices.why: That puts a browser engine under a native app to run one sum, which is not what the lesson describes.

choices.text: Nothing can do it; native means everything twice
choices.why: Shared logic with native screens is exactly what Kotlin Multiplatform offers.

prompt: node screen-web.ts stops with ReferenceError: document is not defined. Which line failed?

choices.text: The import of planner.ts
choices.why: The import worked; the error points further down.

choices.text: The call to weekTotal
choices.why: weekTotal ran: it is plain TypeScript with no DOM in it.

choices.text: The last line, where drawWeek is called with an empty plan
choices.why: That line is in the stack trace because it called drawWeek, but the error is thrown inside it, at document.

choices.text: The first use of document
choices.why: Right: line 6, document.createElement. Node.js has no page.

prompt: screen-term.ts draws the week, marks s3 done and draws it again. How many minutes are done in the second line?
Where, besides a browser, does screen-web.ts run as it is?

choices.text: In a React Native app
choices.why: React Native's screen is the platform's views; there is no document.

choices.text: In a wrapper's WebView
choices.why: Right. A WebView is a browser engine and makes a page.

choices.text: In a Flutter app
choices.why: Flutter's screen is its own engine's surface, and Flutter runs Dart.

choices.text: In Node.js, once the types are stripped
choices.why: The types were stripped; the capture shows it failing at document.

prompt: planner.ts goes unchanged into a React Native app because it has no ___ in it, only rules.
A team of web developers has a working site and four weeks to be in both stores, and the app needs nothing beyond the camera. Which approach fits what the lesson describes?

choices.text: Native, because the camera needs Kotlin and Swift
choices.why: The camera is covered by plugins and libraries in every approach; writing two apps is the slowest route.

choices.text: A web wrapper, with a camera plugin
choices.why: Right. It keeps the site they have, goes to both stores, and a plugin reaches the camera.

choices.text: Kotlin Multiplatform, to share the site's logic
choices.why: The site is JavaScript; Kotlin Multiplatform would mean rewriting it in Kotlin and drawing two native UIs.

choices.text: A PWA, because it is in both stores automatically
choices.why: A PWA has no app package and no store of its own.

prompt: Which of these need code written in Kotlin or Swift somewhere? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A Flutter app using a sensor no plugin supports yet
choices.why: Yes: the host side of the platform channel is Kotlin and Swift.

choices.text: A Kotlin Multiplatform app's iOS screens
choices.why: Yes, unless Compose Multiplatform draws them: native iOS screens are SwiftUI.

choices.text: A PWA installed from the browser
choices.why: A PWA is a website; there is no native code at all.

choices.text: lesson 1's planner.ts running in a React Native app
choices.why: It is plain TypeScript and needs nothing native.
